The slide decks ship with [MCQ check-ins](slides/index.html). This page is for **everything else** you might do to get students talking: prediction prompts, peer teaching, error analysis, four-corners polling, stop-and-jots. Each prompt has a stated time budget and the kind of room arrangement that works best.

::: {.callout-tip title="Mix one in every 15-20 minutes of lecture"}
Empirically, undergrad attention drops sharply after ~15 minutes of straight lecture ([Bunce et al. 2010](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ed100409p)). One short prompt every 15-20 minutes resets attention and surfaces misconceptions you didn't know students had. They don't have to be elaborate — a 60-second "turn to your neighbor and explain X" works.
:::

## Prompt formats used below

| Format | What it does | Time | Setup |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prediction** | Before showing the result, ask students to predict it. Surfaces priors. | 1-3 min | Index card or chat poll |
| **Pair-and-share** | Pairs explain a concept to each other; instructor picks one to share out. | 3-5 min | Any room |
| **Think-pair-share** | Solo think → discuss → share. Slower; deeper. | 5-8 min | Any room |
| **Error analysis** | Show broken code/output; students diagnose. | 5-10 min | Any room with screens |
| **Four corners** | Post 4 claims around the room; students walk to the one they most agree with; defend. | 5-10 min | Movable room |
| **Stop-and-jot** | 90 seconds of silent writing; collect or use as next-class warmup. | 2 min | Any room |
| **Peer teach** | Groups of 3; each person owns one subtopic; teach round-robin. | 10-15 min | Any room with tables |
| **Concept map** | Add today's topic to a running concept map on the board. | 5 min | Whiteboard |

---

# Chapter 1 — Getting started with data in R

**P1.** *Prediction (1 min).* "Before I show you R: how do you think it stores a column of values like `c(1, 2, 3)`? Sketch it on your card." Then reveal the vector with `glimpse()`. (Surfaces spreadsheet priors.)

**P2.** *Pair-and-share (3 min).* "In your own words: what's the difference between R the language and RStudio the program?" After 90 seconds, one volunteer explains; class corrects. (Targets the #1 first-week confusion.)

**P3.** *Error analysis (5 min).* Show a code chunk with `library(dpylr)` (typo). "What's the error message going to say, and what should the student do?" (Builds debugging mindset early.)

**P4.** *Stop-and-jot (2 min).* "Write down ONE question you have about R or RStudio that you'd be embarrassed to ask in class." Collect anonymously; address top 3 next class.

**P5.** *Four corners (8 min).* Post 4 corners: "I've programmed before", "I've used Excel/Google Sheets a lot", "I'm comfortable with high-school math", "None of the above". Students walk to the most-true. Mix groups for first lab. (Builds belonging; informs scaffolding.)

**P6.** *Concept map start (3 min).* On the board, draw a single node: "Data". Ask students to add neighboring nodes for what they think you'll cover this semester. Keep the board photo; revisit in Ch 11.

---

# Chapter 2 — Data visualization

**P1.** *Prediction (2 min).* Before showing a scatterplot of `gapminder` (gdpPercap vs lifeExp), ask: "Will the relationship be positive, negative, flat, or non-monotonic? Predict, then justify." Then reveal.

**P2.** *Think-pair-share (5 min).* "Look at this same plot. What's ONE thing you'd change about it before showing it to your boss?" Pairs compare; share 3-4 ideas with class. (Sets up ggplot polish for the rest of the term.)

**P3.** *Error analysis (5 min).* Show: `ggplot(penguins) + geom_point(aes(bill_length, body_mass), color = species)` (which fails). Ask: "Why is R unhappy?" Hint at *setting* vs *mapping*. (Anchors the `aes()`-vs-non-`aes()` distinction.)

**P4.** *Four corners (8 min).* Post 4 plot types around the room (bar chart, scatterplot, boxplot, line chart). Read a research question aloud ("How has US life expectancy changed since 1900?"). Students walk to the plot they'd build. Defend. Repeat with 2-3 more questions. (Builds chart-choice intuition.)

**P5.** *Pair-and-share (3 min).* "When was the last time you saw a misleading chart in the news? Describe it to your neighbor." Share 2 examples; class diagnoses what made each one misleading. (Hooks into the ethics scenarios for Ch 11.)

**P6.** *Peer teach (12 min).* Groups of 3. Each person owns one geom (`geom_point`, `geom_line`, `geom_bar`). They teach the other two how it works using the same dataset. Round-robin. (Cements the "grammar" idea.)

---

# Chapter 3 — Data wrangling

**P1.** *Prediction (2 min).* Show `flights |> filter(month == 12) |> nrow()`. Ask: "What will the answer be approximately — closer to 100, 1000, 10000, or 100000?" Reveal. (Builds numeric intuition for dataset sizes.)

**P2.** *Stop-and-jot (3 min).* "Write a sentence in plain English describing what this pipe does: `flights |> filter(carrier == 'UA') |> group_by(origin) |> summarize(n = n())`." Pair to compare. (Forces translation; surfaces pipe confusion.)

**P3.** *Error analysis (5 min).* Show: `flights |> select(month) |> filter(flights$month == 12)`. Why doesn't this work? (Targets the "we're already inside the pipe" misconception.)

**P4.** *Concept map (5 min).* On the board, list the 6 core `dplyr` verbs. Ask students to add a real-world analogy for each (filter = TSA letting people through; select = picking dishes off a menu; mutate = ...). Photo for review.

**P5.** *Pair-and-share (4 min).* "Your partner is going to give you a data question; you write the pipe. Then swap." Sample questions on slide: "Which carrier has the longest mean delay?", "How many flights left after 10pm?", "What's the most common destination?"

**P6.** *Peer teach (15 min).* Groups of 4. Each person owns one operation: filter, mutate, group_by + summarize, the `*_join()` family. Each teaches with a 2-minute mini-demo. (Saves you from lecturing on joins.)

---

# Chapter 4 — Data importing and tidy data

**P1.** *Prediction (2 min).* "Tidy data is data where each row is ___, each column is ___, and each cell is ___." Have students fill in the blanks before you reveal Wickham's three rules.

**P2.** *Stop-and-jot (3 min).* "Draw two versions of the same 6-row mini-dataset: one tidy, one untidy. Label which is which." Pair to compare; instructor picks one strong example for the class.

**P3.** *Four corners (8 min).* Post 4 datasets (printed mini-tables) around the room, only one of which is actually tidy. Students walk to the one they think is tidy and defend. (High-energy; surfaces every misconception about "long" vs "wide".)

**P4.** *Error analysis (5 min).* Show output from `read_csv()` where dates parsed as character and one column has trailing whitespace. "What went wrong, and what would you check next?" (Real-world skill.)

**P5.** *Pair-and-share (3 min).* "Find a dataset on your phone (camera roll, Spotify, fitness tracker). What would 'tidy' look like for that data?" Share 3 examples. (Bridges to real life.)

**P6.** *Concept map (4 min).* Add "tidy data" to the running map. Where does it connect — to wrangling? to visualization? Most importantly, what depends on it later (every modeling chapter)?

---

# Chapter 5 — Basic regression

**P1.** *Prediction (3 min).* Show a scatterplot of `mtcars` (mpg vs wt) WITHOUT a fitted line. Ask: "If I fit `lm(mpg ~ wt)`, what's the SIGN of the slope? Estimate the SLOPE in mpg per 1000 lbs. Estimate the INTERCEPT." Reveal; discuss who was close and how they got there.

**P2.** *Pair-and-share (5 min).* "Explain in your own words: what does the residual for a single observation tell you?" Pairs trade; one volunteer summarizes for class. (Targets the #1 regression-week sticking point.)

**P3.** *Error analysis (5 min).* Show R output where a categorical predictor has a confusing reference level ("Why does Asia show up in some places and not others?"). (Anchors the reference-level idea before it bites.)

**P4.** *Four corners (8 min).* Post 4 claims: "R² measures how good my prediction is", "R² measures how strong the relationship is", "R² is the percent of variation explained", "R² tells you if the model is right". Walk to the truest. Defend. Reveal the nuance. (R² is widely misunderstood; surface it.)

**P5.** *Stop-and-jot (3 min).* "Write one sentence translating the regression equation $\\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x$ into English, using a real variable name (`temp`, `price`, `flipper_length`...)." Collect 2-3; reveal. (Builds the unit-aware interpretation habit.)

**P6.** *Peer teach (12 min).* Groups of 3. Each person owns one of: intercept interpretation, slope interpretation, residual interpretation. Round-robin teach using the same fitted output. (Distributes the explainer work.)

---

# Chapter 6 — Multiple regression

**P1.** *Prediction (3 min).* "When we add a second predictor to a regression, the coefficient on the first predictor often CHANGES. Predict: will it usually get bigger, smaller, flip sign, or it depends?" Reveal: "it depends — that's the whole point". (Sets up confounding.)

**P2.** *Think-pair-share (8 min).* Show two regressions: simple `lm(price ~ size)` slope = +$200/sq-ft, then multiple `lm(price ~ size + condition)` slope on size = +$150/sq-ft. "What changed and why?" Pairs; share-out. (Surfaces the "controlling for" intuition without you lecturing on it.)

**P3.** *Error analysis (5 min).* Show a regression with two highly correlated predictors and inflated SEs. Don't explain — ask: "What looks weird here?" Lead them to multicollinearity. (Pre-Ch 11 inference-aware students will spot it.)

**P4.** *Four corners (8 min).* Post 4 model specifications for the same dataset (`y ~ x1`, `y ~ x1 + x2`, `y ~ x1 * x2`, `y ~ x1 + x2 + x1:x2`). Students walk to the one they'd recommend; defend. (Forces explicit thinking about interactions.)

**P5.** *Pair-and-share (4 min).* "Explain to your partner: what does the slope on `size` MEAN in `lm(price ~ size + condition)`?" Listen for "holding condition constant" / "after controlling for condition" phrasings. (The whole chapter rides on this phrase.)

**P6.** *Stop-and-jot (3 min).* "Write the regression equation for `lm(price ~ size + condition)` where condition has 3 levels. How many slopes? How many intercepts?" Collect; reveal. (Builds the dummy-variable intuition.)

---

# Chapter 7 — Sampling

**P1.** *Prediction (3 min).* "I'm going to sample 50 balls from a bowl that's 30% red. About what % red would you predict your sample to be? Now write down the range you'd expect across 20 different samples." Reveal sampling distribution. (Anchors variability.)

**P2.** *Pair-and-share (5 min).* "Explain to your partner: WHY does sample size affect the precision of an estimate?" Listen for hand-wavy answers; push toward "averaging cancels out noise". (Surfaces the LLN intuition before naming it.)

**P3.** *Four corners (10 min).* Post 4 sampling schemes for a campus poll: "ask everyone in your dorm", "ask everyone in stats class", "ask people walking past the library", "ask a random sample from the registrar". Walk to "least biased". Defend. Re-poll after discussion. (Real-world bias intuition.)

**P4.** *Error analysis (5 min).* Show a tweet claiming "97% of users prefer X based on our online poll." Ask: "What's wrong with this claim?" (Bridges to ethics scenarios.)

**P5.** *Concept map (4 min).* Add to running map: "population", "sample", "statistic", "parameter", "sampling distribution". Draw the arrows. (Most students confuse statistic vs parameter — surface it now.)

**P6.** *Stop-and-jot (3 min).* "What's the difference between a sampling distribution and a data distribution? Use the bowl example." Collect; review next class. (Targets the second-week sticking point.)

---

# Chapter 8 — Confidence intervals

**P1.** *Prediction (2 min).* "If I run a 95% CI 100 times on 100 different samples, how many CIs do I expect to contain the true parameter?" Most will say 95. Push: "Is it EXACTLY 95? Why or why not?"

**P2.** *Four corners (10 min).* Post 4 claims: "95% means there's a 95% probability the parameter is in this CI", "95% means 95% of CIs from repeated samples would contain the parameter", "95% means I'm 95% confident in the estimate", "95% means 95% of the data is in this interval". Walk to the right one. (THE classic CI misconception; address head-on.)

**P3.** *Error analysis (5 min).* Show a CI that's $(2, 50)$ — very wide. Ask: "What does this tell you about the analysis? What would you do to narrow it?" (Targets the "always increase n" reflex while reviewing what affects CI width.)

**P4.** *Pair-and-share (5 min).* "Your partner is a journalist. Explain what a confidence interval is, without using the words 'probability' or 'statistical'." (Forces lay-language; surfaces who really gets it.)

**P5.** *Stop-and-jot (3 min).* "Why does the bootstrap work — i.e., why is resampling from a sample a reasonable proxy for sampling from a population?" Collect; review. (Bootstrap is magic-feeling; demystify.)

**P6.** *Concept map (4 min).* Add to map: "point estimate", "interval estimate", "bootstrap", "sampling distribution". How do they connect to last week's chapter? (Cumulative wiring.)

---

# Chapter 9 — Hypothesis testing

**P1.** *Prediction (2 min).* "I'm going to flip a coin 20 times. If it's fair, predict the most extreme outcome you'd want to see before suspecting it's biased." Most say 15-16 heads. Show simulation; reveal that 14+ already starts being unusual at $\\alpha = 0.05$. (Calibrates intuition vs formal cutoffs.)

**P2.** *Four corners (10 min).* Post 4 statements: "A small p-value proves the alternative is true", "A small p-value means the result is important", "A small p-value means the null is unlikely given the data", "A small p-value means the data is unlikely under the null". Walk to the right one. (The MOST classic statistics misconception.)

**P3.** *Pair-and-share (5 min).* "Explain Type I and Type II error to your partner using a medical-trial analogy." (Forces concrete grounding; surfaces who confuses the two.)

**P4.** *Error analysis (8 min).* Show 3 scenarios:
- p = 0.06, n = 10
- p = 0.04, n = 10000
- p = 0.0001, but the practical effect is 0.1% improvement

"Rank these by 'evidence' AND by 'importance'. They're not the same." (Surfaces the significance-vs-importance distinction.)

**P5.** *Stop-and-jot (3 min).* "If you fail to reject the null, can you conclude the null is TRUE? Why or why not?" Collect; review. (Common error in student writing.)

**P6.** *Peer teach (15 min).* Groups of 4. Each person owns one step of `infer`'s pipeline: `specify()`, `hypothesize()`, `generate()`, `calculate()`. Each demos on the same dataset. Then group does a full pipeline together. (Replaces 30 min of lecture.)

---

# Chapter 10 — Inference for regression

**P1.** *Prediction (2 min).* "If I have $n = 1000$, a 95% CI for my regression slope will be (narrower / wider / about the same) than the same CI with $n = 100$. Justify." Reveal; tie to SE formula.

**P2.** *Four corners (10 min).* Post 4 residual plots (random scatter, fan shape, curved pattern, S-shape). Read a model out loud. Walk to "which residual plot matches what we'd expect if our model is GOOD". (LINE diagnostics live or die on visual recognition.)

**P3.** *Pair-and-share (5 min).* "Explain: if a regression slope has p < 0.001, can we say the predictor CAUSES the outcome?" Listen for nuance about randomized vs observational; correlation vs causation. (Sets up Ch 11.)

**P4.** *Error analysis (8 min).* Show a regression where theory-based and bootstrap CIs disagree substantially. "What does the disagreement tell you?" (Builds the "trust the bootstrap when LINE breaks" instinct.)

**P5.** *Stop-and-jot (3 min).* "Which of LINE conditions can a residuals-vs-fitted plot diagnose? Which can it NOT?" Collect; review. (The most over-relied-on plot in the chapter.)

**P6.** *Concept map (5 min).* Connect: "regression line" (Ch 5) — "uncertainty in the slope" (Ch 10) — "p-value" (Ch 9) — "CI" (Ch 8). Most students never see how these connect; draw it for them, or have them draw it.

---

# Chapter 11 — Tell your story with data

**P1.** *Stop-and-jot (5 min).* "Pick one chart you've made this term. Write 3 things you'd improve about it for a non-technical audience." (Self-critique; sets up the polish theme.)

**P2.** *Four corners (10 min).* Post 4 versions of the same headline chart (different titles, axis labels, color choices, annotation). "Which would you put in a report? Why?" (Real instinct for what 'communication' means.)

**P3.** *Pair-and-share (5 min).* "Your partner is a stakeholder. Pitch your project's headline finding in 90 seconds, no jargon. They'll ask one clarifying question." Swap. (Practices the executive-summary muscle.)

**P4.** *Error analysis (8 min).* Show a "data story" report that overclaims: causal language from observational data, no uncertainty stated, cherry-picked window. Have students mark up what's wrong. (Bridges to ethics scenarios.)

**P5.** *Peer teach (15 min).* Groups of 3-4. Each owns one phase: question → data → analysis → communication. Walk through their (or each others') project that way. (Reinforces the pipeline frame.)

**P6.** *Concept map closing (8 min).* Bring back the Ch 1 photo of the "Data" concept map. Add every concept from this term to it. Compare to start-of-term map. (Powerful close to the course.)

---

## Adapting these prompts

**Smaller classes (<25)**: pair-and-share and stop-and-jot are easiest; share-outs feel natural.

**Larger classes (>100)**: prefer four-corners (with hand signals if no movable seats), polling tools (Mentimeter, PollEv, or `learnr` if you have a class server), and stop-and-jots (collected via online form).

**Asynchronous / online classes**: stop-and-jots become discussion-board posts; four-corners becomes a poll; pair-and-share becomes a 5-minute breakout room.

**TAs running discussion sections**: see the [TA guide](ta-guide.html) for per-chapter section scripts that build on these prompts.
